newsitem.title: USA: Citadel women cadets decide not to return.
newsitem.headline: Citadel women cadets decide not to return.

text.p: Two women cadets who alleged their clothing was set on fire by upperclassmen at the Citadel military college announced on Sunday they would not return for their second semester.
Kim Messer and Jeanie Mentavlos, who were among four women enrolled after the school changed its all-male admissions policy last summer, said in separate statements that they would not be returning.
Cadets were due to return to the college by Sunday night.
A Citadel spokesman said the school would have no comment on the decision until a news conference on Monday.

At the heart of the female cadets' decision not to return were allegations that they were sprayed with fingernail polish remover and set afire. Neither cadet was injured in the alleged incidents, reported in December.
After the reports, the U.S. Justice Department and the parents of the women demanded extra security and asked the school to hire outside help as it adjusts to women.

Messer said the Citadel administration was "incapable of impressing on some of its cadets what is expected of every member of the United States military -- the requirement that they obey the law and follow orders."
In her statement, Mentavlos said she had been promised by the Citadel that "knob (freshman cadet) life would be rough but safe."
"Because the Citadel broke its promise, I cannot return to the Corps of Cadets," she said.
"I was told that the chain of command stretched from the bottom to the top. Nobody told me that the chain of command might not be followed when the cadets decided to rewrite the rules," she said.
Mentavlos' brother, Michael, a senior cadet, also announced he would not return to the school but would seek to complete his degree requirements elsewhere.
Messer said in her statement that she never asked for special treatment at the Citadel.
"However, I received special treatment. Special treatment by way of criminal assaults, sadistic illegal hazings, and disgusting incidents of sexual harassment," she said.
In a hearing last week, U.S. District Judge Weston Houck, who presided over the Citadel's admission of women, urged the school to increase safety measures.
Citadel Commandant Joseph Trez assured the court at the hearing that the school planned better security when classes resumed, including a supervisor in each of the four barracks.

The Citadel said last week that 11 cadets had been charged with school violations in the alleged hazing. Those charged include two cadets temporarily suspended from campus and five cadet officers removed from the barracks where the women lived. Punishment could range from marching tours to expulsion.

The Citadel began admitting women after the U.S. Supreme Court last year ruled unconstitutional single-gender education at publicly funded Virgina Military Institute, the only other state-funded all-male military college in the country.

In 1993, Shannon Faulkner sued the Citadel to become its first female cadet, but dropped out during the first week of classes in 1995 before being officially sworn in as a cadet, citing stress and isolation.
She was admitted under court order before the Supreme Court ruled in the VMI case.
